sec.title: Background
sec.p: Lip and oral cavity cancer (LOCC) remains a significant issue in Europe, with an uneven public health burden. While trends have shifted, regional and sex-specific disparities persist due to modifiable risk factors. Using Global Burden of Disease 1990 to 2023 estimates, this study evaluates long-term trends and projects Europe's future LOCC burden.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Study data of 2023 were examined to evaluate the trends of incidence, prevalence, and mortality of LOCC in Central, Eastern, and Western Europe. We conducted a retrospective analysis of age-standardized incidence (ASIR), prevalence (ASPR), and mortality rates (ASMR), alongside disability-adjusted life years (ASDR). Trends over time were examined using Joinpoint regression to estimate average Annual Percent Change (AAPC:). Furthermore, ARIMA time-series models were employed to generate future burden for the period 2024 to 2033.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: From 1990 to 2023, Europe showed a clear East-West divide in LOCC. Western Europe successfully lowered its death rates (AAPC: −1.08%) and disability rates (AAPC: −1.41%). However, Central and Eastern Europe saw new cases rise (AAPC: 0.63% and 0.60%) along with more alcohol-related deaths. The highest burden was in Russia and Hungary, where male DALYs rate reached 207 per 100,000. ARIMA forecasting shows this gap will grow by 2033; while Central Europe’s ASIR is expected to fall to 4.65 per 100,000, Eastern Europe’s prevalence is projected to rise to 18.12 per 100,000 population.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Europe highlights widening variations in LOCC burden, with Western Europe achieving substantial progress while Central and Eastern Europe face continuous worsening trends;

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Lip and oral cavity cancer (LOCC) represent a significant and growing global public-health challenge within the spectrum of head-and-neck malignancies. Cancer remains one of the leading causes of death worldwide, with an estimated 20 million new cases and 9.7 million cancer deaths in 2022, and oral cancers continue to contribute substantially to this burden.1 LOCC principally encompasses malignant epithelial tumours arising from the vermilion lip and oral cavity, including cancers of the lip, floor of mouth, anterior tongue, gums, hard palate, and other specified intraoral sites.2,3 Globally, LOCC remains a huge major issue resulting in almost 0.378 million new cases and 0.178 million deaths worldwide in 2020. This disease has a significant impact particularly on men, persons aged 50 years and older, and populations with substantial exposure to tobacco, alcohol, or UV radiation.4, 5, 6 Estimates from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Study indicate that the incidence, deaths, and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) associated with LOCC have exceed twice the values of 1990 to 2021, with an increase in the age-adjusted incidence rate in the globally, though some regions have experienced a plateau in.7 These increasing trends have underlined the contemporary public health significance of LOCC, particularly in regions with sustained exposure to major preventable risk factors.

Europe carries a disproportionately large burden of cancers compared to its population size, with more than 4.4 million new cases in 2022, making the study of site-specific cancers such as LOCC within the region’s heterogeneous epidemic profile.8 As per GBD 2021, Western Europe has shown an absolute health burden with 14,280.66 death and 41,940.55 incidence cases, despite maintaining the lowest mortality rate of 1.56. Conversely, Central Europe exhibited the most severe proportional impact with the highest death rate of 2.86 and an incidence rate of 5.27, even though its absolute counts were the lowest at 6,001.88 deaths and 10,819.68 cases. GLOBOCAN 2022 data demonstrate substantial regional heterogeneity in the incidence of lip and oral cavity cancer across Europe, with Central Europe showing the highest incidence burden. This region forms a clear high-incidence cluster, with Slovakia (7.26 per 100,000) and Portugal (7.2).9 Epidemiological studies consistently show marked divergence in lip and oral cavity cancer burden across Europe, with Central and Eastern European countries reporting notable higher incidence and mortality than those in Western Europe.10,11 These differences have been associated to diverging patterns of alcohol consumption, tobacco use, socioeconomic transitions, occupational exposures, and health-system capacity for early detection. Most previous studies lump Europe together or mix oral cavity with oropharyngeal cancers, making it hard to see LOCC across European sub-regions.12, 13, 14

The recent GBD 2023 cancer estimates (1990-2023) give the possibility to reassess LOCC trends with updated methods and expanded forecasting capacity.15,16 Therefore, this study aims to comprehensively analyse current burden, the trends, and future projections of lip and oral cavity cancer in Central, Eastern, and Western Europe from 1990 to 2023, using the GBD Study 2023. This study providesinter-regional comparative assessment of incidence, mortality, DALYs, and risk-factor contributions.Italso intends to generate policy-relevant awarenessfor targeted prevention efforts to strengthen cancer-control strategies in Europe.

sec.title: Overview
sec.p: This study utilized data from the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study GBD 2023, a comprehensive systematic analysis that quantifies health loss across 204 countries and territories. The GBD 2023 framework provides standardized estimates for 375 diseases and injuries, 292 distinct causes of death, and 88 behavioural, environmental, occupational, and metabolic risk factors.17 In estimating the burden of lip & oral cavity cancer, a very wide range of data is considered in the GBD 2023 framework, including national vital registration systems, population-based cancer registries and verbal autopsy records. Estimates of mortality were produced by a model called Cause of Death Ensemble (CODEm), that considers various models in a systematic approach aimed at providing predictions that are optimized given the available covariates. Because cancer registration is often more complete for mortality than incidence in many regions, incidence was back-calculated from mortality estimates using mortality-to-incidence ratios (MIRs). Non-fatal outcomes, including prevalence and years lived with disability (YLDs), were modelled using DisMod-MR 2.1, a Bayesian meta-regression tool that ensures internal consistency across all epidemiological parameters. DALY is a measurement of this total burden that considers both years of life lost (YLL) to early deaths and years of living with disease (YLD). All health estimates are reported with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs) and follow the Guidelines for Accurate and Transparent Health Estimates Reporting (GATHER) to ensure methodological transparency and reproducibility.

sec.title: Selection of countries
sec.p: In accordance with the GBD study 2023 regional classification, Europe was stratified into three analytical regions: Central Europe (13 countries), Eastern Europe (7 countries), and Western Europe (24 countries). The Central European region comprised Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Czechia, Hungary, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Poland, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia, and Slovenia. Eastern Europe included Belarus, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, the Republic of Moldova, the Russian Federation, and Ukraine. The Western European region encompassed Andorra, Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Iceland, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Luxembourg, Malta, Monaco, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, San Marino, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom.

sec.title: Data sources
sec.p: All data were obtained from GBD 2023 (https://vizhub.healthdata.org/gbd-results/) dataset. The age-standardized rates of incidence, prevalence, mortality, and DALYs, including years of life lost (YLLs) and years lived with disability (YLDs) were calculated as primary outcomes in the study. Lip and oral cavity cancer was defined according to ICD-10 codes C00 and C02-C06, encompassing malignancies of the lip and specified intraoral sites. The main predictors were European subregion (Central, Eastern, Western Europe) and calendar year (1990-2023).17 Thevariables were analysed as age-standardized rates per 100,000 population using the GBD reference population. Boundary maps of lip and oral cavity cancer in Europe were created using QGIS to display 2023 age-standardized Incidence, prevalence, DALYs and mortality rates.18 The uniform case definitions and model-techniques ensured comparability across European regions, and study years. To validate the reliability of the current burden, GBD 2022 incidence estimates were cross-referenced with the GLOBOCAN 2022 dataset (https://gco.iarc.who.int/today).19 A comparative analysis was performed for across 41 nations to ensure that GBD rates align with registry-based observations. The uniform case definitions and model-techniques ensured comparability across European regions and study years.

sec.title: Statistical methods
sec.p: To analyse long-term trends in incidence, prevalence, mortality, and DALY rates for LOCC, the join point regression model was employed. This method identifies segments in trend data, allowing for a detailed linear trend analysis. It computes:(1)APC:i={exp(βi)−1}×100
Average Annual Percent Change (AAPC:) across the full period:(2)AAPC:i={exp(∑wiβi∑wi)−1}×100
Where: i denotes the number of segments
βi represents the regression coefficient for each segment
widenotes the duration of each corresponding segment

The grid search method (GSM) was employed to identify the number and locations of joinpoints. Model selection was optimized using the Monte Carlo permutation test and the modified Bayesian information criterion (BIC), with preference given to the model yielding the lowest mean squared error. APC: is a unitless relative measure that shows the direction and speed of change; a negative APC: or AAPC: (where the upper bound of the 95% confidence interval is less than zero) indicates a downward trend. A positive APC: or AAPC:, with the lower bound of the 95% CI above zero, shows a trend of increase. When the 95% CI includes zero, it represents a stable trend, with no statistically significant change over the period of time. We compared the GBD 2022 age-standardized incidence rates directly with the GLOBOCAN 2022 dataset for all 41 nations. This comparison was performed to identify apparent potential regional disparities in the reported data across Europe.

Future trends in LOCC were projected using autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) models for 2024 to 2033. This stochastic time-series approach is well suited to oncological data, as it captures complex temporal dynamics including evolving trends and random variation that may be missed by simpler linear models.20 The ARIMA (p, d, q) framework integrates autoregressive (p) and moving average (q) terms following differencing of order (d) to achieve stationarity, which was confirmed using the Augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) test. The ARIMA (p, d, q) model can be mathematically represented as follows:(3)Δyt=c+∑i=1pϕiyt−i−∑j=1qθjet−j+et
Where c is a constant, et is a white noise et∼N(0,σ2), ϕ=(ϕ1,ϕ2,…,ϕp) and θ=(θ1,θ2,…,θq) are the vector of model coefficients.

The best model selections for each region and demographic group were found by minimizing Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and BIC to achieve the most parsimonious fit. To assess the predictive performance of the forecasts, we calculated established accuracy metrics, specifically the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) and the root mean square error (RMSE). While thoroughly investigating the residuals of these models to verify they were close to white noise. All statistical analysis was done by using RStudio software (version 4.3.0) and Microsoft Excel software (Version 2310).Trends in disease burden over time were analyzed using Joinpoint Regression Program software, (version 5.2.0), which provided APC: values as well as average APC: values.21 Comparisons of sex subgroups were made across Central Europe, Eastern Europe, and Western Europe to examine regional differences using QGIS (version 3.44.0-Solothurn).22,23

sec.title: Age-standardized incidence rates (ASIR) for lip and oral cavity cancer
Age-standardized prevalence rates (ASPR) for lip and oral cavity cancer
sec.p: Western Europe consistently recorded the highest ASPR, though the trend has remained constant, as indicated by the non-significant APC:, which was 0.02% (P > .05), However, the prevalence rates in Central and Eastern Europe showed a substantial rise over time, as detailed in Table 1. The joinpoint analysis indicated steady growth in Central Europe from 1990 to 2015 (P < .01), followed by stabilization. There were several points of change in Eastern Europe, six in total, but nonetheless, there was steady growth (AAPC: P < .001).As shown in Figure 1, Western Europe's ASPR has been fluctuating, with a rise that rise and decreased in mid-period but increased in more recent years, so that there is a modest overall trend (AAPC: 0.22%, P < .001).

sec.title: Age-standardized DALY rates (ASDR) for lip and oral cavity cancer
sec.p: In Western Europe, the greatest improvement in overall disease burden was seen, with significant long-term trend reductions in DALYs (AAPC: −1.41%, P < .001). This trend, consistent with a number of negative APCs in the period 1990 to 2021 illustrated in Table 1,is a representation of the decline in health loss. The rate of decline was slower in central Europe with an initial significant increase (APC: 1.58%, P < .01), stabilization through the mid-2000s, and significant declines thereafter (APC: −0.66% and −1.48%; both P < .05), producing a modest downward AAPC: (-0.14%, P = .0012). The Eastern Europe region experienced both rising and falling rates over various periods, resulting in near-stable long-term DALY trends (AAPC: 0.08%, P > .05). The greatest improvement over a decade took place in the Western Europe region between the years 2000 and 2010, as depicted in Figure 1.

sec.title: Age-standardized mortality rates (ASMR) for lip and oral cavity cancer
sec.p: Mortality trends mirrored DALY patterns. Western Europe showed the most significant and persistent decline (AAPC: −1.08%, P < .001), which was underpinned by negative APC: for several join points.Central Europe presented an initial increase (APC: 1.09%, P < .01), followed by a period of stability and significant decrease from 2006 onwards (APC: −0.15% and −1.37%; both P < .05), leading to a relatively stable trend over the long-term period (AAPC: 0.02%, P > .05). Eastern Europe followed an irregular trend with rises and falls over six join points to attain stability (AAPC: 0.09%, P > .05). In comparison by 2023, Western Europe continued to have the lowest mortality rate; thereafter, Central & Eastern Europe was significantly higher than Western Europe, indicating inequities in survival (Figure 1 & Table 1).

sec.title: Geographic variation in sex-specific age-standardized burden indicators for lip and oral cavity cancer
sec.p:
The gender-specific regional distribution of the age-standardized disease burden for Europe in the year 2023 is shown in Figure 2. In men: The range of ASIR cases per 100,000 was between 2.7 and 12.9. The highest rates were seen in France at 12.9 per 100,000, 12.2 at Hungary, and 10.5, whereas Nordic nations such as Finland with 3.1 and Norway with 2.7 had the lowest rate; for females, the range for ASIR varied from 1.16 to 5.18 per 100,000, with higher rates reported for the United Kingdom at 5.1 and Iceland at 4.8, while lower rates were observed for Ukraine at 1.8 and Bulgaria at 1.2. ASPR rates (Figure 2B)have shown that for men, prevalence reached its peak in South western and Western Europe, with the greatest prevalence in Portugal at 73.0 per 100,000 and Spain at 68.5, in contrast to Northern regions, such as Finland at 12.3 per 100,000 and Estonia at 15.1 recorded significantly lower levels; female prevalence mirrored this geographic trend, with higher concentrations in the United Kingdom and Southern Europe. In contrast, age-standardized DALY rates (Figure 2C) and mortality rates (Figure 2D) showed a clear East-West gradient, with a difference in male DALYs from 25 to 207 in 100,000 in Russia at 207, Ukraine at 185, and Hungary at 172, while Spain at 25 and Norway at 28 had the lowest rates. Age-standardized mortality for males peaked in Hungary at 6.78 per 100,000 and Romania at 6.21, contrasting with Sweden at 0.96 and France at 1.12. For females, DALYs between 7.9 and 42.4 per 100,000 and mortality between 0.27 and 1.64 per 100,000 were highest in Poland and Russia, whereas Southern European nations like Spain and Greece consistently reported the lowest female mortality and DALY burdens.Fig. 2

sec.title: Burden of risk factors: alcohol and tobacco
sec.p:
Figure 3 shows the comparative burden of lip and oral cavity cancer caused by tobacco and alcohol use in three European regions from 1990 to 2023. Looking at the Age-Standardized DALY rates (Figure 3A), the burden from tobacco dropped a lot in Western Europe, falling from 28.74 to 12.98 per 100,000. Central Europe stayed the region with the highest burden, even though its rate decreased from 37.42 to 30.68 per 100,000. On the other hand, DALYs caused by alcohol dropped sharply in Western Europe (15.53 to 7.96 per 100,000) but went up slightly in Central Europe (15.41 to 15.70 per 100,000) and Eastern Europe (12.83 to 13.81 per 100,000). These trends are also found in the ASMR (Figure 3B), where there were significant decreases in tobacco-related deaths in Western Europe from 0.94 to 0.46 per 100,000 and in Central Europe from 1.17 to 1.02 per 100,000. Although alcohol-related deaths declined in Western Europe (0.48 to 0.28 per 100,000), they actually rose in Central Europe (0.47 to 0.50 per 100,000) and Eastern Europe (0.37 to 0.40 per 100,000), indicating that alcohol consumption is a steadily increasing concern in these regions.Fig. 3

sec.title: Future projections of the European LOCC burden
Discussion
sec.p: The findings of this study highlight a persistent East-West divide in the LOCC burden across Europe. Joinpoint regression analysis indicates a successful decoupling of prevalence from mortality in Western Europe. While there has been a sustained decline in DALYs (AAPC: −1.41%) and mortality rates driven by a significant reduction in modifiable risk factor exposure the prevalence rates in the West remain high and stable. This sustained high prevalence is a 'survivorship effect' resulting from superior oncological care, earlier diagnosis, and improved survival rates compared to other regions. The results of the study demonstrate substantial and concerning regional variation in the observed trends with respect to the risk-attributable burden of disease; Western Europe is characterized by a substantial reduction of alcohol-attributable deaths and DALYs for the period 1990 to 2023, whereas the disease burden increases over the same period in Central and Eastern Europe. This reveals that alcohol is a major and presumably increasing public health problem with respect to lip and oral cavity cancer in these regions. Most importantly, our forecast up to 2033 indicates that, although the ASIR is expected to decrease in Central Europe (from 5.1 to 4.65 per 100,000), the ASPR in Eastern Europe is forecasted to increase to 18.12 per 100,000. These diverging trajectories, driven by the disproportionate burden of alcohol in the East and the aging population, highlight the point that unless drastic region-specific policies interventions, the health geographical disparity in LOCC burden are poised to widen over the next decade. Currently, few studies have systematically examined the burden of LOCC across Central, Eastern, and Western Europe using the latest GBD 2023 estimates. Moreover, only limited prior research has compared temporal patterns, risk factor–attributable burden, and projected trends across these specific European sub-regions.

The study done by Sung et al (2021) similarly ascribed growing cancer incidence in transitioning regions to ongoing behavioural risks and demographic ageing.24 Western Europe consistently shown the highest ASIR in 2023, but maintained a marked long-term drop, which reflects the effectiveness of better prevention systems and strong oral cancer care.The prevalence patterns emphasize the variations in the east-west regions of Europe. Central and Eastern Europe revealed marked upward progressions in prevalence, resembling the findings with Liu X et al (2025), who reported increasing global ASPR especially in middle-SDI regions caused by rising incidence and inadequate mortality decline.25 On the other hand, Western Europe exhibited the highest ASPR yet remained stable long term, indicating improved survival and efficient follow-up care. Above all, our study found that emerging survivor burden in Central and Eastern Europe coexists with stagnant improvements in mortality, highlighting an expanding unmet need for survivorship and rehabilitation support.

The burden of disease is estimated by using the ASMR and ASDR.26 The ASDR was decreased sharply in Europe’s Western region, especially from 2000 to 2010; but Central region of Europe revealed moderate continuing decline and Eastern Europe was relatively stable. The study by Bernabe E & et al, 2025 mentioned that DALY-decline was associated with high-sustainable development index (SDI) regions, while low and moderate-SDI regions shown the stability or surge.27 The findings of Harris et al (2021) indicated the unequal DALY rise in moderate and high-human development index (HDI) regions, especially Eastern region of Europe.28 As like DALY pattern, the Western Europe also displayed the continued decline of the ASMR but stability in Eastern and Central Europe. The study done by Sofi-Mahmudi et al has shown that Global Quality of Care Index (QCI) highest in Western Europe, but lower QCI gains in low-SDI regions parallel the stagnant mortality trends we found in the Eastern-Europe.29 This supports the role of system-level vigilance and early detection in reducing the mortality. The previous studies indicated the higher burden of DALY and ASMR in males because of alcohol and tobacco exposure.30,31 Our study also shown the sex-specific variations with higher DALY and ASIR in males but Central Europe with emerging female burden due to lifestyle changes, HPV, and metabolic risks.

In this study, we found that the geographic variation within Europe revealed significant country-level variations. In Europe, the highest prevalence was observed in Western countries (Portugal, the United Kingdom, and France), while the highest mortality occurred in Eastern countries such as Belarus and Romania. Oral disease burden among older adults shows marked disparities by sex, age, SDI, and region, underscoring the need for targeted prevention and resource allocation.32 Ghanem et al (2025) and the GBD 2019 LOCC analysis mentioned the highest incidence of LOCC in high-SDI regions, while the highest mortality & DALYs in lower middle-SDI regions.16,33 This affirms again the importance of socio-demographic development in influencing cancer outcomes, thereby confirming the significance of accessible cancer treatment in European regions of lower-resource. We found the diverging APC: trends across Europe with wanning in the west while increases in the east highlight the broader disparities in access to early detection and rational treatment. The major risk factors to LOCC burden found were alcohol and tobacco. The regional variation in LOCC burden observed in this study is significantly influenced by the distribution of modifiable risk factors, particularly the synergistic relationship between alcohol consumption and tobacco use. As established by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC),34 alcohol is a Group 1 carcinogen that facilitates the development of oral malignancies. This effect is profoundly amplified when combined with tobacco smoking; evidence suggests that heavy concurrent users face up to a 35-fold higher risk35,36 for oral cancer mortality compared to non-users. Addressing these overlapping risk factors through region-specific policy interventions remains critical to mitigating the projected rising burden in Eastern Europe. Oral cancer mortality trends and geographic patterns also appear to be related to changes in alcohol consumption. The exceedingly high rates in Hungary and in a few other countries of Eastern Europe can be related not only to the overall quantity of alcohol consumed but also to the drinking pattern and to the type of alcohol consumed.37 Eastern and Central Europe shown consistent rising burden, while Western Europe revealed the sharpest declines in DALYs and mortality due to these risk factors. These findings match with Pérez Jardón et al (2025) findings, who highlighted the alcohol and tobacco control and the need for early detection at dentist-level.38 Akashanand et al (2024) and Zhang et al (2022) reported the important role of prior behavioural control policies so as to decline the disease burden due to sustained tobacco and alcohol exposure.30,39 In Europe, it has been estimated that approximately 75% of oral cavity cancers occur as a result of a combination of alcohol and tobacco as causative agents.40

Our projections for 2024 to 2033 demonstrate the diverging future directions. The Western Europe is projected to sustain declines in DALYs and mortality with stable incidence. However, the Eastern Europe is expected to rise the prevalence & mortality with stable incidence, suggesting ongoing high-risk exposure, inadequate early diagnosis, and slower treatment-system evolution. The Central Europe is expected to decline the incidence and DALYs with stable mortality. These predictions closely correspond with the GBD 2019 results, where the prevailing burden of LOCC in the Resource-limited settings corresponds with alcohol, tobacco, and undetected screen failures.16 Liu Y et al (2025) additionally projected that ASIR and ASDR would continue to rise worldwide, especially in mid-SDI countries.41

This study provides a comprehensive assessment of the LOCC burden across Central, Eastern, and Western Europe, utilizing standardized GBD 1990 to 2023 data and robust analytical methods, including Joinpoint regression, age-standardization, and ARIMA forecasting. By identifying these sub-regional areas, this study reveals the significant heterogeneity that is often masked in more general continental analysis, and by integrating country-level mapping, risk-factor stratification, and sex-based trends, the relevance to policy-level interventions is greatly magnified. Most notably, these findings indicate widening regional disparities, with clear progress observed in Western Europe, contrasted by increasing incidence and prevalence and stagnant mortality in Central and Eastern Europe, highlighting the need for expanded oncology capacity and improved early detection strategies. The strong regional concordance between GBD estimates and GLOBOCAN 2022, particularly the high-incidence clustering in Central Europe, supports the robustness of our findings. In a direct comparison of age-standardized incidence rates, our GBD estimates showed remarkable alignment with GLOBOCAN’s registry-based figures in nations such as Belarus, where GBD estimated a rate of 6.32 compared to GLOBOCAN’s 6.38. Minor differences between the two datasets likely reflect inherent distinctions between national registry reporting and GBD estimation frameworks, as well as potential regional misclassifications of cases within specific sub-national health systems.

However, these findings should be interpreted considering several limitations. The use of secondary GBD data introduces natural limitations within the findings concerning the level of diagnostic validity for cancer and completeness, and reporting quality across European countries, which might also affect comparability at the regional level. Furthermore, this study relies on the regional groupings defined by the GBD 2023 study; any inherent misclassification of countries within these predefined GBD regions may influence the comparative results between Central, Eastern, and Western Europe. Moreover, the fact that the sub-regions had never before been systematically studied made it impossible to compare the results to longitudinal evidence. Methodologically, reliance on modelled estimates rather than primary clinical or individual-level exposure data may attenuate short-term variability and limit the assessment of individual-level risk heterogeneity. Finally, this analysis does not incorporate sub-national variation regarding health system structures, such as, differences in screening compliance or disparities in treatment availability, which probably affect the noted epidemiologic trends.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Lip and oral cavity cancer is a serious concern in Europe, exhibiting an escalating gap between East and West. Although there has been a decrease in deaths and DALYs in Western Europe, there has been an increase in ASIR in Central and Eastern Europe due to persistent risk factors. Our GBD 1990 to 2023 analysis and Joinpoint regression reveal these disparities, while ARIMA forecasting predicts this divergence will intensify through 2033. This trend threatens SDG Target 3.4, which aims to reduce premature NCD mortality by one-third by 2030. To meet these goals, Europe must implement region-specific tobacco and alcohol controls, enhance oncology capacity, and strengthen early-diagnosis systems to ensure equitable health progress.

sec.title: Data availability
sec.p: The data used in this study were obtained from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 results tool maintained by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME). All indicators for lip and oral cavity cancer in Central, Eastern and Western Europe (incidence, prevalence, DALYs and mortality) can be accessed free of charge from the GBD results portal (https://vizhub.healthdata.org/gbd-results). And GLOBOCAN 2022 cancer incidence estimates are available from the Global Cancer Observatory of the International Agency for Research on Cancer (https://gco.iarc.fr/en). No additional, unpublished primary data were generated or analysed for this study.

sec.title: Ethics statement and consent to participate
sec.p: This study used aggregated, de‑identified data from the publicly available Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 database and did not involve direct contact with human participants or access to individual‑level records. Hence, formal ethical approval and informed consent were not required for this secondary analysis of open‑access data.

sec.title: Declaration of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the writing process
sec.p: Artificial intelligence tools were used only to assist with grammar checking, formatting checks, and language refinement during manuscript preparation. No content, ideas, data, statistical analysis, figure generation, or scientific conclusions were created by AI tools; all study design, data interpretation, and final text were developed and verified by the authors.
